senses.gloss:
Tsaru,--(a) This word seems to denote some sort of crawling animal in one passage of the Rigveda.
(b) In the later literature the word means a ‘handle,’ as of a beaker (camasa). In this sense also it seems to occur in the description of the plough (lāṅgala) in the Atharvaveda and the later Saṃhitās.
Foot notes vii. 50, 1. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 99.
pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa, xxv. 4. Cf. Lāṭyāyana Srauta sūtra, x. 12, 12, etc.
iii. 17, 3, where the ordinary text has soma-satsaru (so the pada text), and the Paippalāda recension has somapitsalam.
taittirīya Saṃhitā, iv. 2, 5, 6, has sumati-tsaru; Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, ii. 7, 12; kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xvi. 12; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xii. 71; vasiṣṭha dharma sūtra, ii. 34, have somapitsaru, which vasiṣṭha renders as ‘provided with a handle for the drinker of Soma’ (i.e., somapi-tsaru). Weber, Indische Studien, 17, 255, suggests soma-sa-tsaru, ‘with (sa-) strap (uman, a conjectural word) and handle’ (tsaru). Whitney, Translation of the Atharvaveda, 116, prefers to read throughout sumati-tsaru, ‘with well-smoothed handle,’ from the root seen in matī-kṛ, etc. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 236; Bühler, Sacred Books of the East, 14, 13.

Tsārin denotes, in one passage of the Rigveda, a ‘hunter’ engaged in the chase of the takva (an unknown beast), according to Ludwig and Max Müller. But this explanation is quite conjectural.
Foot notes i. 134, 5.
Sacred Books of the East, 32, 448.
